King's Gambit.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.f4 — offer a pawn at once to rip open the f-file and attack.
King's Gambit.idea: White gives up a pawn for speed and an open f-file. If Black takes, build a big centre and hunt the king; if Black declines, develop fast and keep the attack.

Vienna Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 — a flexible start that can turn into a fast f4 attack.
Vienna Game.idea: Develop the knight first, keep f4 in reserve. White stays flexible: quiet development, or a sharp kingside push when Black is careless.

Bishop's Opening.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 — put the bishop on its best diagonal before the knight.
Bishop's Opening.idea: The bishop eyes f7 right away. White keeps options for d4 or f4 later and avoids the heavy theory of the Ruy Lopez and Italian.

Center Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 — grab the centre and bring the queen out early.
Center Game.idea: White trades the centre pawn and develops the queen fast, accepting that Black will gain tempi hitting it. Simple play, but the queen must not be careless.

Danish Gambit.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 — sacrifice pawns for two open bishops and speed.
Danish Gambit.idea: White gives one or two pawns so both bishops aim at Black's king. If Black returns the extra material correctly, White is fine; if not, the attack comes quickly.

Elephant Gambit.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 — hit the centre at once, even at the cost of a pawn.
Elephant Gambit.idea: Black fights for the centre immediately. It is risky against good play, so the aim is to get active pieces and punish a careless White.

Philidor Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 — a solid wall of pawns and slow counterplay.
Philidor Defense.idea: Black defends e5 with a pawn, keeps a compact setup and waits. It is passive, but hard to break if you know the typical plans.

Latvian Gambit.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 — an all-in counterattack with a big hole on f5.
Latvian Gambit.idea: Black attacks White's centre on move two and accepts weaknesses. Good practical chances against beginners, risky against theory.

Damiano Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 — a famous bad move; the point is to know why.
Damiano Defense.idea: 2...f6 weakens the king. Against it, White can sacrifice on e5 and win quickly. Study it to avoid, or to punish it as White.

Ruy Lopez.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 — pressure the knight, the centre and squeeze slowly.
Ruy Lopez.idea: The Spanish is the classic main road: pin the defender of e5, castle, and build up the centre step by step. Slow squeeze, rich in plans.

Italian Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 — a natural setup aiming at f7, easy to learn.
Italian Game.idea: The bishop eyes f7 and White builds with c3 and d3 or d4. Great for beginners because the ideas are simple and the development is natural.

Ponziani Opening.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 — prepare d4 and take a big centre.
Ponziani Opening.idea: White supports a strong d4 push before Black can react. It is less known than other open games, so opponents often lack preparation.

Scotch Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 — open the game right away and fight for the centre.
Scotch Game.idea: White trades the d-pawn to open lines early. Active pieces and a lead in space instead of slow manoeuvring.

Scotch Gambit.oneLiner: 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 — give the pawn back later for fast development.
Scotch Gambit.idea: Instead of recapturing, White develops the bishop and castles, aiming at f7 while Black's pieces are still at home.

Göring Gambit.oneLiner: 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 — sacrifice a pawn to open lines for the pieces.
Göring Gambit.idea: White offers a pawn for fast development and open lines against Black's king. If Black declines with ...d5, White still gets a healthy centre.

Three Knights Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 — simple, solid development with both knights.
Three Knights Game.idea: Develop both knights, then choose a plan: d4, Bb5 or Bc4. A quiet way to reach a playable open game.

Four Knights Game.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 — symmetrical and very safe for both sides.
Four Knights Game.idea: Both sides develop all four knights. White can play the Spanish pin, or the Scotch push d4 for an open game.

Petrov Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 — mirror White's attack with a counterattack.
Petrov Defense.idea: Black attacks e4 instead of defending e5. Drawish at top level but with many traps for White who captures on e5 carelessly.

Sicilian Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 c5 — fight for the centre without copying White; unbalanced and sharp.
Sicilian Defense.idea: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, gaining the open c-file and counterplay. The most popular reply to 1.e4 for players who want to win.

Pterodactyl Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5 — an offbeat queen sortie in the Sicilian.
Pterodactyl Defense.idea: Black brings the queen out early to a5 to hit e5 and the c3 square. Unusual and tricky, but White gets a lead in development.

French Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 e6 — build a solid pawn centre and hit White's with ...d5.
French Defense.idea: Black accepts a cramped bishop on c8 for a rock-solid structure. The plan is to attack White's centre with ...c5, then play for counterplay.

Caro-Kann Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 c6 — a very solid reply that keeps the bishop free.
Caro-Kann Defense.idea: Black prepares ...d5 with a pawn on c6, so the light bishop can develop outside the pawn chain. Safe, sound and good for endgames.

Scandinavian Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 d5 — challenge the centre at once, queen out early.
Scandinavian Defense.idea: Black hits e4 immediately. After the exchange the queen recaptures and must be placed carefully. Few theoretical lines to learn.

Pirc Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 — let White build a centre, then attack it.
Pirc Defense.idea: Black fianchettos the bishop and strikes at the centre later with ...c5 or ...e5. A flexible, hypermodern defence.

Modern Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 g6 — fianchetto first, decide the pawn structure later.
Modern Defense.idea: Black delays the central fight and puts the bishop on g7. Very flexible, but White gets space, so react at the right time.

Alekhine Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 Nf6 — invite White's pawns forward, then attack them.
Alekhine Defense.idea: The knight provokes e5, and Black hopes White's advanced pawns become targets. Rich, unbalanced and tricky for both sides.

Nimzowitsch Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 Nc6 — develop a knight first and keep the centre flexible (includes rare side-lines).
Nimzowitsch Defense.idea: Black delays the central pawn decision and aims for ...e5 or ...d5 later. Offbeat, so it often leaves White without preparation.

Owen's Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 b6 — fianchetto the queen's bishop against White's centre.
Owen's Defense.idea: The bishop on b7 pressures e4 from afar. White gets space, but Black stays flexible and solid.

St. George Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 a6 — a tricky waiting move that prepares ...b5.
St. George Defense.idea: Black plans a queenside fianchetto and a flexible centre. Unusual, so White must think for themselves early.

Rat Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 — wait, then react to White's setup.
Rat Defense.idea: A flexible way to reach Pirc and Modern structures. Black keeps options open and avoids sharp theory.

Lion Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 — the Philidor with a quick knight.
Lion Defense.idea: Black fights for the centre with ...e5 right away and develops the knight to d7. Solid and easy to understand.

Borg Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 g5 — an extreme, offbeat reply to confuse the opponent.
Borg Defense.idea: Black pushes the g-pawn on move one. Risky and unsound against best play, but you should know how to handle it.

Queen's Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 — offer a pawn to win control of the centre.
Queen's Gambit.idea: White challenges d5 with the c-pawn. If Black takes, White regains the pawn and gets a strong centre; if not, White keeps a space advantage.

Queen's Gambit Accepted.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 — take the pawn, then give it back for freedom.
Queen's Gambit Accepted.idea: Black takes the c-pawn and aims for ...c5 and quick piece play. The pawn is usually returned, with an equal position.

Queen's Gambit Declined.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 — hold the centre with a solid pawn on e6.
Queen's Gambit Declined.idea: Black refuses the pawn and keeps the d5-pawn supported. Solid and classical, with the problem bishop on c8 to solve.

Slav Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 — defend d5 and keep the bishop free.
Slav Defense.idea: Black supports d5 with the c-pawn and plans ...Bf5 before closing the centre with ...e6. A sturdy, reliable choice.

Semi-Slav Defense.oneLiner: 2...c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 — a sharp mix of the Slav and the QGD.
Semi-Slav Defense.idea: Black builds a solid centre but accepts a blocked c8-bishop. The Meran and Botvinnik lines lead to very sharp, double-edged play.

Albin Counter-Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 — sacrifice a pawn for quick activity.
Albin Counter-Gambit.idea: Black strikes at White's centre right away and gets a strong d4-pawn if White is not careful. Tricky with many traps.

Chigorin Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 — develop a piece and fight the centre with pieces.
Chigorin Defense.idea: Black develops the knight before the pawns and ignores classic centre rules. Unusual and rewards creative play.

Baltic Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 — get the bishop out early, before ...e6.
Baltic Defense.idea: Black develops the light bishop outside the pawn chain at once and keeps a solid structure.

London System.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 — an easy-to-learn setup that works against almost anything.
London System.idea: White develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, plays e3, c3 and Nf3. Few theory lines to memorize, with solid structure.

Colle System.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 — a quiet build-up before an e4 break.
Colle System.idea: White sets up pawns on d4/e3/c3, develops the bishop to d3 and prepares e4. Easy to learn, with a clear plan.

Torre Attack.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 — pin the knight, build solidly.
Torre Attack.idea: The bishop on g5 pins the f6-knight. White follows with e3 and Nbd2, a simple system for many opponents.

Trompowsky Attack.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 — avoid main-line theory by attacking the knight at once.
Trompowsky Attack.idea: White pins or trades the knight to damage Black's structure and reaches unusual positions early.

Richter-Veresov Attack.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 — develop actively and keep an edge in activity.
Richter-Veresov Attack.idea: White puts pieces on active squares and avoids main lines. Good for players who prefer ideas to theory.

Stonewall Attack.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 and f4 — a solid pawn wall with a kingside attack.
Stonewall Attack.idea: White builds pawns on d4, e3, c3 and f4, then attacks on the kingside with the bishop on d3. A plan, not a list of moves.

Blackmar-Diemer Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.e4 — sacrifice a pawn, rip open the f-file, and hunt the king.
Blackmar-Diemer Gambit.idea: White offers a pawn with e4 and f3 for open lines and a quick attack. Objectively Black can hold, but the practical chances are big.

Englund Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 e5 — a trappy gambit that sets quick tricks.
Englund Gambit.idea: Black sacrifices a pawn to bring the queen out and hunt for traps. Dangerous only if White plays carelessly.

English Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 — queen's bishop fianchetto against d4 and c4.
English Defense.idea: Black aims at the centre with the bishop on b7 and keeps flexible pawn structure choices.

Dutch Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 f5 — fight for e4 with the f-pawn, aim for the attack.
Dutch Defense.idea: Black takes control of e4 and aims for a kingside attack. The weakened king means you must develop carefully.

Nimzo-Indian Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 — pin the knight and fight for e4.
Nimzo-Indian Defense.idea: Black develops with a pin and aims to double White's pawns. One of the soundest and most respected defences to 1.d4.

Queen's Indian Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 — control e4 with the bishop on b7.
Queen's Indian Defense.idea: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to fight for e4 and the centre. Solid and flexible.

Bogo-Indian Defense.oneLiner: 3.Nf3 Bb4+ — an early check that avoids the Nimzo pin theory.
Bogo-Indian Defense.idea: Black checks and trades or retreats the bishop, reaching safe positions without needing a lot of theory.

Catalan Opening.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 — fianchetto the bishop for long-term pressure.
Catalan Opening.idea: White's bishop on g2 presses on the long diagonal against b7 and the queenside. A strategic opening with a small, lasting edge.

King's Indian Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 — let White build a centre, then attack it.
King's Indian Defense.idea: Black fianchettoes and strikes with ...e5 or ...c5. Great for attacking players who like a kingside storm.

Grünfeld Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 — hit the centre with ...d5 at once.
Grünfeld Defense.idea: Black challenges White's centre immediately and attacks it with the bishop on g7 and ...c5. Sharp and theoretical.

Benoni Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 — unbalanced fight with a queenside majority.
Benoni Defense.idea: Black gives White the centre but gets queenside pawn majority and the long diagonal for the g7-bishop. Sharp, double-edged.

Old Benoni Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 c5 2.d5 d6 — an older, simple way to play the Benoni.
Old Benoni Defense.idea: Black counters White's centre with the c-pawn and keeps the position flexible. White gets a space advantage.

Benko Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 — give a pawn for long-term queenside pressure.
Benko Gambit.idea: Black sacrifices the b-pawn to open files for the rooks and bishop. The pressure remains even in endgames.

Old Indian Defense.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 — a solid setup with ...e5 to follow.
Old Indian Defense.idea: Black builds a compact structure and aims to strike in the centre later. Safe, if a little passive.

Budapest Gambit.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 — sacrifice a pawn for quick piece play.
Budapest Gambit.idea: Black gives up a pawn on e5 but gets rapid development and chances for a quick regain with activity.

English Opening.oneLiner: 1.c4 — control d5 from the flank and keep the position flexible.
English Opening.idea: White controls the centre with a flank pawn and transposes into many structures. A strategic opening for players who like flexibility.

Réti Opening.oneLiner: 1.Nf3 — develop first and control the centre from a distance.
Réti Opening.idea: White fianchettos and strikes in the centre later with c4. Flexible, with a hypermodern feel.

Zukertort Opening.oneLiner: 1.Nf3 followed by quiet development — flexible and often transposes.
Zukertort Opening.idea: White keeps the central structure open and decides later. Many move orders lead to well-known systems.

King's Indian Attack.oneLiner: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3 — one setup against almost everything.
King's Indian Attack.idea: White uses the same set-up whatever Black does, then plays e4 and attacks on the kingside. Little theory to remember.

Bird's Opening.oneLiner: 1.f4 — seize e5 with the f-pawn and play for a kingside attack.
Bird's Opening.idea: White controls the e5 square and builds a Dutch-like setup in reverse. It weakens the king a little, but it is uncommon and surprising.

Nimzo-Larsen Attack.oneLiner: 1.b3 — long-diagonal pressure with the bishop on b2.
Nimzo-Larsen Attack.idea: White develops the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and fights for the centre with pieces. Flexible and less studied.

Van Geet Opening.oneLiner: 1.Nc3 — a flexible first move that can transpose to many systems.
Van Geet Opening.idea: White develops a knight first and decides on the structure later. A good surprise weapon.

Barnes Opening.oneLiner: 1.f3 — a weird, weakening first move; mostly a trap to avoid.
Barnes Opening.idea: 1.f3 blocks the knight and weakens the king. Know the dangers, and know that Black can exploit it quickly.

Irregular Openings.oneLiner: Rare first moves: a3, a4, b3, b4, c3, d3, e3, g3, g4, h3, h4, Nc3, Nh3.
Irregular Openings.idea: Uncommon first moves for surprise value. Most are sound enough but give Black a comfortable game if met with sensible central play.

Black Knights' Tango.oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 — an offbeat reply that avoids main-line theory.
Black Knights' Tango.idea: Black attacks the centre with the knights before choosing a pawn structure. White gets space, but must know the tricks around ...Nb4/...Nd4.

Scholar's Mate Defense.oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 or 2.Qh5 — an early attack on f7 that looks like instant mate. Stay calm.
Scholar's Mate Defense.idea: Do not panic and do not grab material. Chase the queen with ...g6 and ...Nc6, then guard f7 with ...Nf6 or ...Qe7. Once the queen is pushed back, the attack runs out of steam and you are fine.

Hedgehog System.oneLiner: 1.c4 c5 or 1.Nf3 Nf6 — a solid set-up with ...e6, ...b6 and a bishop on b7.
Hedgehog System.idea: Build a wall with ...e6 and ...b6 and point the bishop down the long diagonal. Wait for the right moment, then open the centre with ...cxd4 or ...d6. Keep the knights flexible and the queenside pawns in reserve.
